year.label: 1987-1989 BMW M3 (E30) FIA Group A touring car racing specification

records.real_world_identity_notes: Kunos's own bundled Assetto Corsa content (documented through the community Assetto Corsa Mods wiki and assetto-db.com, both of which read the game's own internal data rather than guessing) separates this content - internal id bmw_m3_e30_gra, ~290+ bhp, 945 kg, dogleg-H transmission - from a distinct sibling content, "BMW M3 E30 DTM" (internal id bmw_m3_e30_dtm, researched separately as issue-103), which represents the later, most extreme 1990-1992 Class 1 DTM specification with a non-dogleg H-pattern 6-speed gearbox and permitted ABS. Independent motorsport-history sources (TouringCarTimes, Iconic Auctioneers, the BMW M heritage site) corroborate that BMW Motorsport's Group A M3 raced from 1987 (Roberto Ravaglia's inaugural World Touring Car Championship title that year) through 1989 at roughly 300 hp from the 2.3-litre S14 engine, campaigned via Works-supplied body shells prepared by Schnitzer (Germany), Prodrive (UK) and others to FIA Group A Touring Car regulations, before the DTM's 1990 move to 2.5-litre, up-to-360 hp Sport-Evolution-based cars. This car's ~290 bhp in-game figure sits within that earlier 1987-1989 range rather than the later, more extreme spec, so record_action is create-new rather than reusing the existing curated data/v1/cars/bmw-m3-sport-evo-group-a.json record, which is a different simulator's (AMS2) representation of the precisely-dated 1990 M3 Sport Evolution homologation special - the final and most extreme E30 M3 evolution. No exact single season or chassis is stated anywhere reviewed for this AC content, so the year is reported as the 1987-1989 range rather than a single year. The car's transmission is well corroborated across a primary FIA homologation form and multiple independent secondary sources as a Getrag 265 five-speed dogleg-pattern synchromesh manual, consistent with (though not necessarily identical in every part to) the same core Getrag 265 unit used across the model's Group A racing life.
records.confidence_basis: Manufacturer, model, and the general 1987-1989 Group A touring car racing identity are corroborated across the game's own community-documented internal data (Assetto Corsa Mods wiki, assetto-db.com), independent motorsport-history sources (TouringCarTimes), and period-context auction-house material (Iconic Auctioneers) that all describe the same car: BMW's factory-supported Group A M3 (E30) touring car racer. No existing curated record in this repository targets this specific, earlier (pre-1990) Group A specification, so record_action is create-new.

records.specification_basis: The FIA homologation form tabulates five-speed gearbox sets for this car, a secondary drivetrain comparison independently names a Getrag 265 five-speed, and a classified listing for an actual Getrag 265/5 unit built for Group A racing gives a full five-ratio table, with no reviewed source proposing a different forward gear count for this (as opposed to the six-speed DTM sibling) content. Every five-forward-gear gearbox set homologated on this FIA form is explicitly marked synchronised. The form does homologate other, six-speed gearboxes of differing (including unstated or blank) synchro construction, but this car has five forward gears, so no choice is being made between homologated options at that gear count. The remaining step, from what the form permits to what this specific car was built with, is inferred rather than directly stated, which keeps this at medium rather than high confidence. The community wiki's own infobox for the exact bundled content explicitly states a Dogleg-H transmission for this ("STD") variant, as distinct from the separate "DTM" variant's plain H-pattern six-speed. The FIA homologation form's gate diagram and independent secondary sources both describe a gated, lever-operated manual, consistent with an H-pattern gate rather than a sequential or paddle mechanism. The community wiki explicitly names this variant's gate "Dogleg-H". The FIA homologation form's section 603(f) draws the gate with reverse above first and 1/3/5 on the lower plane - a dogleg with first down and left - and independent secondary sources, including a classified listing for the exact gearbox unit, consistently describe it as a dogleg. The FIA homologation form's section 603(f) gate diagram places reverse above first, with first, third and fifth on the lower plane, putting first down and to the left of the racing shift plane. Every reviewed source describes a conventional foot-clutch, gated manual gearbox for this car, with no mention anywhere of an automated or clutchless launch system on any Group A-era example. A gated dogleg manual of this type requires the driver to operate the clutch to move off. Derived from the established H-pattern dogleg manual construction: a gated manual of this era and type is shifted with the clutch as authentic technique. This follows from the established mechanism rather than being independently stated for upshifting specifically, which keeps this at medium rather than high confidence. Derived from the established synchromesh H-pattern construction: a clutched manual upshift on a gearbox of this type requires lifting the throttle to unload the drivetrain for the shift. This is standard technique for the established mechanism rather than something a source states about this car specifically. Derived from the established H-pattern dogleg manual construction: a downshift on a gearbox of this type is made with the clutch, as authentic technique. Follows from the established mechanism rather than a direct downshift-specific statement, hence medium rather than high confidence. A synchromesh gearbox matches shaft speeds itself, so a downshift blip eases the synchros and is authentic technique but is not required to engage the gear. This follows from the established synchromesh construction rather than being separately stated by a source, so it cannot exceed the medium confidence of that underlying construction finding. The full-resolution interior photograph shows a continuous, round, black three-spoke rim with no fixed grip humps or flattened section. Confidence is kept low because the source is an explicitly modern recreation built up from a 1991 production shell rather than a photograph of an original 1987-1989 works or privateer race car. The photograph shows the rim's upper section continuing unbroken around the top of the wheel rather than being cut away. Confidence is kept low for the same recreation-car caveat as the shape finding. The photograph shows all instrumentation (a bank of analog dials in a red-faced panel) mounted on the dashboard rather than the wheel; the wheel itself carries no LCD, LED numeric readout, or other rim-integrated display. Confidence is kept low for the same recreation-car caveat as the shape finding. The photograph shows no LED or lamp array mounted on the wheel rim itself. Confidence is kept low for the same recreation-car caveat as the shape finding. The reviewed sources did not establish the remaining technique and wheel fields, which stay unknown in the real-car baseline: /authentic_controls/transmission/upshift/automatic_cut, /authentic_controls/transmission/upshift/manual_blip, /authentic_controls/transmission/upshift/automatic_blip, /authentic_controls/transmission/downshift/throttle_lift, /authentic_controls/transmission/downshift/automatic_cut, /authentic_controls/transmission/downshift/automatic_blip.
